articles.description:
Originally published on the Cloud ex Machina engineering blog.
A Terraform security scan running on GitHub Actions in an infrastructure repository cost about $2 every time someone merged to the main branch. Nobody looked at a number that small. At 48 merges a week it came to about $4,800 a year, roughly three quarters of the repository's CI bill, and most of that money paid to re-check code that had been checked minutes earlier. Scanning only what each merge changed brought the same check down to $126 a year. The fix was one pull request, and the hard part was getting the cost in front of the people who write CI, a group that now includes coding agents.

A workflow author sees a green check and a duration on each pull request, and hears about it fast when a workflow gets slow, because peop…
articles.title: A CI security scan cost $4,800 a year, and nobody who wrote it saw the bill

articles.author: Artyom
articles.description:
Agent benchmarks ask how well an agent follows its instructions. We wanted to ask one step up: how good are the instructions in the first place?
Agents are getting good at doing what they're told. Give a current model a clear policy and the right tools and it mostly sticks to it, which is exactly what benchmarks like τ-bench measure. So the weak link is moving upstream. Someone has to write that policy, and the person who knows the business is rarely the person who knows how to write rules a machine can act on. A gap in a policy doesn't throw an error, either. The agent follows the incomplete policy faithfully and the customer just gets the wrong outcome.
Once you trust your agent as an executor, the next question is how you know your instructions are any good. We think that's one of the m…

You finish a 14-page report, hit "Save as PDF", and the file lands at 23 MB. You try to attach it. Gmail warns you, Outlook rejects it, the client's portal times out at 10 MB.

Duplicated fonts. Every font in the document can be embedded…

articles.author: Karlis Gutans
articles.description:
Every Git beginner hits the same wall: the commands are easy to copy, but the picture behind them is missing.
You can type git add, git commit and git push for months without knowing how they connect. Then the first merge conflict arrives, and the copied commands stop helping.
A cheat sheet does not fix this. A cheat sheet is a flat list. Git is a structure: areas, branches, remotes and history that depend on each other.
So I made five mind maps that show the structure: dev-mind-maps.karlis-gutans.workers.dev
Git basics: what Git is, first-time setup, the repository, the three areas, the commit and the daily loop.
Branching and merging: what a branch is, HEAD, working with branches, merging, merge conflicts and a typical workflow.
Working with remotes: clone, fetch, pull, push and the daily rhythm.
History: inspecting, undoing, rewriting and how to stay safe.
Git tools: hosting platforms, GUI clients, editor integration, terminal helpers and automation.
Each topic is split into 4 to 6 short parts.
Each part is one card with one idea.
The last card shows the whole topic in one map.
The site is static: no sign-up and nothing to install.
A list tells you what to type. A map shows where a command sits.
One example: git fetch and git pull sit next to each other on the remotes map. Fetch downloads the new commits. Pull downloads them and merges them into your branch. On a list these are two unrelated lines. On a map the difference is visible at a glance.
The same pages work in a mobile browser. That makes the maps useful for five minutes of revision away from the desk.
I made the maps in my own mind map editor, with Claude Fable 5.2 assistance. If you find a mistake, tell me in the comments and I will fix it.
The same site already has seven Python maps. They get a separate post.
How did you learn Git: commands first, or the picture first? And which Git topic is missing from these five maps?
articles.title: Git in 5 Mind Maps

articles.author: Viswaretas Kotra
articles.description:
Multi-node training means starting one torchrun on every machine, all pointed at the same rendezvous address, so their processes form one group and NCCL averages gradients over the network between them. On Nodus, --nodes 2 --launcher torchrun does that wiring: it acquires the machines, checks they connect and sets MASTER_ADDR, NODE_RANK and the torchrun variables (multi-node is in Beta, with an API ceiling of 8 machines). It only pays when the network can move a step's gradients in about the time the backward pass takes.
This post covers what our multi-GPU training guide skips: what must work between machines, how much data crosses the wire, and what failures look like in our own test.
Two separate connections have to succeed. The first is the rendezvous: every machine's torchrun agent con…
articles.title: How do you run multi-node training across GPU machines?
